title: How a two-sided marketplace should write an about page
excerpt: Use the about page to name who stands behind the offer and why the scarce side should care. Keep the origin story only if it changes the decision to join.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, for an about page that has to name the people behind the offer.
caption: Three cups raised over a wooden table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a marketplace about page prove?
faqs.answer: It should prove that a specific person or role will answer when the scarce side's job goes wrong. Name that role, the promise that reduces their risk, and how to join. A mission statement and a team photo do not replace an owner for applications, payouts, or disputes.

faqs.question: When does a founder story belong on the about page?
faqs.answer: Keep the story when it explains a rule you still enforce, such as a former host who will not let the platform rewrite a menu. Tell it in one paragraph and return to the join path. If deleting the story removes no fact the scarce side needs, the story is for the team, not the page.

faqs.question: Should an early marketplace hide how small the team is?
faqs.answer: Say the truth about who replies and how fast. A founder-run inbox, described plainly, attracts people who can tolerate an early market and warns people who need a large support desk. Update the sentence when the operation changes. A stale name is a broken promise.

markdown:
A two-sided marketplace about page has one job. It proves that specific people stand behind the offer, and it tells the side you need first why that should matter to them. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to join.

The page is not a diary and it is not a culture deck. A stranger who has already seen a match, a fee, and a service still wants a name. Give them the name, the role, and the reason it reduces their risk.

## Proof that someone is accountable

Marketplaces ask the scarce side to take a risk the company cannot fully insure with copy. A host lets strangers into a home. A carrier commits a truck. A worker shows up for a family they have not met. The about page is where that person checks whether anyone will answer when the night goes wrong.

Name the accountable role in the first screen. "Applications are read by Priya, who ran kitchens before this." "Lane disputes go to Andre, who dispatched freight." Use real names only when those people have agreed to be public. If they have not, name the role and the experience without a costume of stock portraits.

Google's people-first guidance treats first-hand experience as a mark of a page worth trusting. On an about page that guidance is literal. The experience to show is experience with this market: years on the tool, years in the job the scarce side does, or a clearly described limit if you are new. "We are obsessed with community" is not experience. "We have seated 40 dinners in one city, and the founder still confirms each menu" is experience, if it is true.

Do not borrow credibility from a team photo in a lobby. A photograph helps when it shows the work, a real room, or a real person who is named beside it. A photograph of hands on laptops in unspecified daylight helps no one decide.

## Why this side should care

The second paragraph of a typical about page turns toward the founder. The scarce side does not care about the founder's childhood unless that fact changes the risk. They care about judgment. Will this company understand a cancellation, a no-show, a spoiled ingredient, a missed dock appointment?

Write three sentences that answer that, in the side's situation. "Hosts set the guest count. We do not add a seat after you confirm." "Carriers name the rate. We do not shop your truck to a lower bidder after you accept." Those sentences belong on the about page because they are promises about character, not about a feature toggle.

Tie each promise to a person or a role when you can. A promise with no owner reads like a policy that will move. A promise owned by the person who answers the phone reads like an operation.

If you are early and the owner is the founder, say so without romance. "You will get the founder until we have a second person on support." That sentence will attract the right early hosts and deter people who need a call center. Both outcomes are useful.

Keep the company's broader mission to a line, after the promises. The mission can be sincere. It is not the reason a careful person joins this month.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns a place when it explains a boundary you still keep. A founder who was a courier and refuses to hide the take rate has a reason to say they were a courier. A founder who hosted dinners and will not let the platform change a menu has a reason to say they hosted dinners. The story is evidence for a rule, not a prelude to the rule.

Tell it short. One paragraph. What you did, what went wrong in the market you came from, what you refuse to repeat. Then return to the side you need first and the join path. A timeline of universities, jobs, and cities is a biography. Biographies are optional. The refusal is not.

Skip the story when it does not change the decision. A pivot from an unrelated app, a weekend in a hackathon, a love of "bringing people together" — none of those tell a host whether their kitchen is safe in your model. Put that material in a founder interview somewhere else if you enjoy telling it. Leave it off the page that is supposed to close the risk.

The test is blunt. Delete the origin section and ask whether the scarce side lost a fact they needed. If they lost nothing, the section was for the team.

## What to leave off

About pages collect leftovers. Cut these unless a sentence of context makes them load-bearing.

A values list with words any company could print: integrity, excellence, customer obsession. If a value changes a behavior, write the behavior and drop the label.

A map of "offices" that are kitchen tables, unless the city matters to the side you are seeding. Then name the city and the hours a person answers, which is the fact hiding inside the map.

Advisor logos and investor names, unless that side would recognize them as a safety signal. A nurse may care that a clinical director reviews applications. A nurse does not care which fund led the round.

Press quotes that compliment the design of the site. The scarce side is not hiring you for the typeface. A quote from a host about a payout that arrived on time is relevant. Use it only if the person said it and is willing to be cited. Do not write a quote you wish they had given.

Award badges you cannot explain in one line. A badge without a reason is jewelry.

## Name the operation, not the vibe

The middle of the page can be a simple account of a week. Who reads applications. Who handles a dispute. What "business days" means in your time zone. How a decision gets reversed if you got it wrong.

This is more persuasive than a culture section, and it is harder to fake, which is why it works. Write only what is true this month. If disputes are a shared inbox the founder checks twice a day, say that. When you hire a dedicated person, change the sentence. Stale about pages are a special kind of false advertising because they name humans.

If the team is one or two people, the page can be short. Length is not proof of substance. A single screen with names, promises, and a join path can outperform a scroll of studio photography. Hanabi's own work pages stay specific for the same reason: a visitor should be able to tell what was made. Your about page should let a host or a carrier tell who will pick up the phone.

Include a way to see the person before the application if that reduces drop-off. A short video of the real reviewer explaining the refusal rules can do more than a paragraph, provided the video is captioned and the rules are also in text. Do not hire an actor. The scarce side is checking for a human, and they can tell.

## Point the page at the decision

End on the join path for the side you need first. The about page is not a cul-de-sac. "Apply as a host" belongs under the promises, with the same label as everywhere else, and with the short list of what to have ready.

Offer the other side a text link, as on the homepage. The about page did not become a neutral plaza just because it is about people. The people you are showing are the ones who serve the side you are trying to earn.

If you mention a city, a credential, or a manual process, make sure the services page and the pricing page say the same thing. Contradictions between "we reply in two days" and "we reply within a week" are more damaging on the about page, because this is the page where you claimed to be accountable.

## Read it once with the other pages open

Print the about page, or read it on a phone with the services page beside it. Highlight every proper noun and every promise that contains a time, a city, or a refusal. Those highlights are the page. If they are thin and the rest is mood, rewrite toward the highlights.

Ask one person from the scarce side, someone who is not an investor, three questions. Who would they contact if a job went badly? What is one thing this company will not do? What should they have ready before they apply? If they cannot answer from the page, add the missing sentence. If they answer from your pitch instead of the page, the page is still a pitch.

Do this before you commission portraits. Pictures of the team are worth paying for after the sentences are true. A polished face next to an empty promise makes the promise look deliberate. Keep one source for the names, too. The about page, the footer, and the note someone receives after they apply should identify the same role. Two inboxes are two policies.

A named team still needs a record of a match that already happened. The next piece is [proof pages for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-two-sided-marketplace), which is where a constraint and a decision replace a portrait.
